title: One Word Substitution
summary: A phrase such as 'murder of a king' must be replaced by one word (regicide). Options are built from suffix families —cide, -phobia, -logy, -cracy, -phile — so classifying the family first kills half the options. The bank below carries 150+ exam-frequency substitutions grouped for daily revision.

subtopics.title: Suffix families: decode the word by its ending
subtopics.concept: In one-word substitution you get a phrase and pick the single word for it. Many answer words are two parts: a root for the object and a suffix for the family. Learn the suffix and you can build the meaning of words you have not seen.

tricks.title: Family first, root second
tricks.body: Read the phrase and name the family (killing, fear, study). Then match the root. Two steps remove most options.

example.q: The study of earthquakes: (a) seismology (b) geology (c) zoology (d) etymology

tricks.title: Stack two families
tricks.body: Rare words are often two parts joined. Nycto + phobia is fear of darkness. Entomo + logy is study of insects.

tricks.title: Make look-alike cards
tricks.body: Write each look-alike pair on one card with the meaning of each word. Revise the cards every week.

mistakes.right: Learn the suffix family and the root. Build the word from two parts.
Entomology is insects. Etymology is word origins.
Father is pater, brother is frater, mother is mater. Check the victim.
Phobia means fear. Phile means love.

mistakes.wrong: Marking a word after reading only its ending.
mistakes.right: Check the root as well. Options often share the same suffix.

subtopics.notes:
### The question and the two-part idea
The question gives a phrase, such as *the killing of a king*. You pick one word: **regicide**.

Most such words have two parts.
- The **root** names the object: reg = king.
- The **suffix** names the family: -cide = killing.

Join them and you get the meaning without memorising the whole word.

### Main families
| Suffix | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -cide | killing | regicide (king), fratricide (brother), patricide (father), infanticide (infant), genocide (a whole race), homicide (a human), suicide (oneself) |
| -phobia | abnormal fear | hydrophobia (water), acrophobia (heights), claustrophobia (closed spaces), xenophobia (foreigners), nyctophobia (darkness) |
| -ology | study of | ornithology (birds), entomology (insects), seismology (earthquakes), etymology (word origins), anthropology (humankind) |
| -graphy | writing, drawing | cartography (making maps), calligraphy (fine handwriting), demography (populations) |
| -phile | lover of | bibliophile (books), philatelist (stamps), anglophile (England) |
| -vorous | eating | herbivorous (plants), carnivorous (flesh), omnivorous (everything), insectivorous (insects) |
| -gamy | marriage | monogamy (one spouse), polygamy (several spouses), bigamy (a second marriage while still married), exogamy (outside one's group) |

> **Tip:** Learn one family a day. Say each word with its object: "reg, king, regicide".

### Roots that name the object
- **reg** king, **frater** brother, **pater** father, **geno** race.
- **hydro** water, **acro** height, **xeno** foreign, **nycto** night.
- **ornitho** bird, **entomo** insect, **seismo** earthquake, **etymo** word origin.
- **biblio** book, **herb** plant, **carn** flesh.

> **Example:** Nyctophobia = nycto (night) + phobia (fear). It means fear of darkness.

### Counting prefixes
These prefixes open many words.
| Prefix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| mono | one |
| bi, duo | two |
| tri | three |
| poly | many |
| pan, omni | all |
| semi, hemi | half |
| cent | hundred |
| milli | thousand |

Omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing) and omnipresent (present everywhere) are one prefix plus one root each.

### How the options are built
A question usually has one right word and three from the same or a nearby family.
- For *study of insects*, the options may all be -ology words. The **root** decides: entomology.
- For *fear of heights*, the options may come from different families. The **suffix** decides: -phobia.

Check both parts every time.

### Look-alike pairs
- entomology (insects) and etymology (word origins).
- patricide (father), fratricide (brother), matricide (mother).
- philatelist (stamps) and numismatist (coins).
- -phobia (fear) and -phile (love).
- astronomy (science of stars) and astrology (predicting from stars).

> **Watch:** Look-alike words differ by one letter group. Read the whole word.

patterns.name: Killing words (-cide)
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'killing of' or 'murder of' and names a victim: king, brother, father, mother, infant, race.
steps: Match the root: reg = king, frater = brother, pater = father.
patterns.why: -cide is the killing suffix. The root names the victim.

example.q: The murder of a king is called: (a) homicide (b) regicide (c) suicide (d) genocide
steps: The victim is a king, so the root is reg.

patterns.name: Fear words (-phobia)
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'an abnormal fear of'.
steps: Match its root: hydro = water, acro = height, xeno = foreign, nycto = night.
Pick the -phobia word with that root.
patterns.why: -phobia is the fear suffix. The root names the thing feared.

example.q: An abnormal fear of heights: (a) claustrophobia (b) hydrophobia (c) acrophobia (d) xenophobia

patterns.name: Study words (-ology)
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'the study of' or 'the science of'.
steps: Match its root: ornitho = birds, entomo = insects, seismo = earthquakes.
Check the look-alikes before you mark.
patterns.why: -ology is the study suffix. The root gives the subject.

example.q: The study of insects: (a) entomology (b) etymology (c) ornithology (d) seismology
steps: Etymology looks alike but means word origins.

patterns.name: Lover, eater and marriage words
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'a lover or collector of', 'feeding on', or describes a marriage practice.
steps: Match the root for the object.
Pick the option with both parts.
patterns.why: Each suffix names a family, and the root names the object.

example.q: One who loves books: (a) bibliophile (b) philatelist (c) anglophile (d) philanthropist

patterns.name: Counting-prefix words
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'all', 'many' or 'one' before the idea (all-powerful, all-knowing).
steps: Find the counting idea: all, many, one, half.
Match the prefix: omni, poly, mono, semi.
Add the root for the rest of the meaning.
patterns.why: One prefix and one root build a whole family of words.

example.q: One who has power to do everything: (a) omniscient (b) omnipotent (c) omnipresent (d) omnivorous

revision: -cide = killing, -phobia = fear, -ology = study, -graphy = writing, -phile = lover, -vorous = eating, -gamy = marriage.
Roots: reg king, frater brother, pater father, hydro water, acro height, xeno foreign, nycto night.
Omni = all: omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent.
Family first, then root.
Look-alikes: entomology/etymology, patricide/fratricide, philatelist/numismatist.

subtopics.title: One word for people: traits, trades and types
subtopics.concept: Most one-word-substitution items start with 'One who' or 'A person who'. They name a person by a job, a habit, a feeling or a situation. Sort them into four boxes and watch out for the partner word planted as a trap.

tricks.title: Object first
tricks.body: Underline the object or habit in the stem before you read the options. It names the family at once.

example.q: One who cannot read or write: (a) illiterate (b) recluse (c) veteran (d) sceptic
steps: The key detail is cannot read or write.
A recluse lives away from people.

tricks.title: Learn words in pairs
tricks.body: Take each word with its partner. Widow goes with widower. Miser goes with spendthrift. The pair is one memory item.

tricks.title: Speak the parts
tricks.body: Say the parts aloud: somn, ambul, ist. Hearing the parts locks the meaning.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing astrologer for 'studies the stars scientifically'.
mistakes.right: Scientific study is astronomer. Foretelling is astrologer.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring the gender word (widow for a man).
mistakes.right: Read man or woman in the stem before you choose.
Miser hoards money. Spendthrift wastes it.
Polyglot knows many languages. Polymath knows many subjects.
Learn each job word with the thing it works on.

subtopics.notes:
### The biggest group
The commonest stem begins with **One who ...** or **A person who ...**. Learn these words in four boxes.

### Box 1: jobs
Learn each job with the thing it works on.
| Word | Job |
|---|---|
| cartographer | makes maps |
| lexicographer | compiles dictionaries |
| cobbler | mends shoes |
| plumber | fits and repairs water pipes |
| surgeon | performs operations |
| dentist | treats teeth |
| oculist | treats eye disorders |
| pharmacist | prepares and sells medicines |
| astronomer | studies stars scientifically |
| astrologer | foretells events from stars |

> **Watch:** The word *scientifically* points to the astronomer. The word *foretells* points to the astrologer.

### Box 2: habits and character
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| teetotaller | never drinks alcohol |
| glutton | eats too much |
| miser | hoards money |
| spendthrift | wastes money |
| gullible | believes everything easily |
| sceptic | doubts everything |
| garrulous | talks too much |
| taciturn | speaks very little |
| misanthrope | hates mankind |
| pedant | shows off his learning |

### Box 3: pairs and opposites
The examiner often puts the partner word in the options.
- widow (woman whose husband has died) and widower (man whose wife has died).
- novice (beginner) and veteran (long experience).
- miser and spendthrift.
- patriot (loves his country) and traitor (betrays it).

> **Tip:** Read the gender or direction word in the stem before you choose.

### Box 4: words built from roots
| Word | Parts | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| polyglot | poly (many) + glot (tongue) | knows many languages |
| somnambulist | somn (sleep) + ambul (walk) | walks in sleep |
| somniloquist | somn (sleep) + loqu (speak) | talks in sleep |
| omniscient | omni (all) + scient (knowing) | knows everything |
| omnipotent | omni (all) + potent (power) | has unlimited power |
| omnipresent | omni (all) + present | present everywhere |
| philanthropist | phil (love) + anthrop (man) | loves mankind |

### More words to bank
- illiterate: cannot read or write.
- recluse: lives shut off from the world.
- martyr: gives his life for a cause.
- apostate: deserts his religion.
- vandal: deliberately damages property.
- arbitrator: hears and settles a dispute.
- biographer writes another person's life. An autobiographer writes his own.

### How to answer
1. Underline the key detail: the object, the habit or the gender.
2. Put the phrase in its box.
3. Choose the option that matches the detail exactly. Reject the partner word and the look-alike.

patterns.name: Person by job
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'one who makes, mends, treats or studies' and names an object or a field.
steps: Recall the job word that goes with it.
patterns.why: Each job word is tied to one object.

example.q: One who makes maps: (a) cartographer (b) lexicographer (c) calligrapher (d) geographer

patterns.name: Person by habit or character
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase describes a habit or nature: never drinks, eats too much, believes anything.
steps: Match it to a character word.
patterns.why: Habit words come in pairs, so the stem detail must be exact.

example.q: One who never drinks alcohol: (a) glutton (b) teetotaller (c) miser (d) sceptic
steps: The habit is not drinking alcohol.
A glutton eats too much. A miser hoards money.

patterns.name: Partner-word trap
patterns.howToSpot: The options hold both members of a pair: widow and widower, miser and spendthrift, novice and veteran.
steps: Find the pair in the options.
Read the gender or direction word in the stem.
patterns.why: The wrong member of the pair is planted to catch quick readers.

example.q: A man whose wife has died: (a) widow (b) widower (c) bachelor (d) veteran

patterns.name: Root-built person words
patterns.howToSpot: The answer is built from Greek or Latin parts: poly, mis, phil, omni, somn.
steps: Match a root to a word in the phrase.
Choose the option that joins the parts.
patterns.why: Two known parts give the whole meaning.

example.q: One who knows many languages: (a) polymath (b) polyglot (c) pedant (d) novice
steps: Polyglot. A polymath knows many subjects.

patterns.name: Look-alike person words
patterns.howToSpot: Two options are one letter apart or share a field (astronomer and astrologer).
steps: Underline the detail word: scientifically or foretells.
Match it to the exact member.
patterns.why: The look-alike is the most common wrong option.

example.q: One who studies the stars scientifically: (a) astrologer (b) astronomer (c) cartographer (d) psychologist
steps: An astronomer studies stars as a science.

revision: Jobs: cartographer maps, lexicographer dictionary, cobbler shoes, plumber pipes.
Habits: miser/spendthrift, garrulous/taciturn, gullible/sceptic.
Pairs: widow/widower, novice/veteran, patriot/traitor.
Roots: poly many, mis hate, phil love, omni all, somn sleep.
Astronomer studies stars. Astrologer foretells from stars.

subtopics.title: One word for places and groups
subtopics.concept: Two question shapes are pure matching. 'A place where X is kept or done' needs a place word. 'A group of X' needs a collective noun. Find the key noun in the phrase and recall its partner.

tricks.title: Animal decides the group
tricks.body: Name the animal in the phrase first. Then recall its one group word.

example.q: A group of wolves: (a) pack (b) pride (c) herd (d) flock
steps: Pride is lions, herd is cattle, flock is sheep.

tricks.title: Sound hooks
tricks.body: Link each look-alike to a sound: api sounds like ape-bee, avi is in aviation. Hooks beat plain rote.

tricks.title: Twenty and twenty
tricks.body: About twenty place words and twenty group words cover nearly every paper. Learn them in one sitting and revise once a week.

mistakes.right: Api goes with bees. Avi goes with aviation and birds.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing cemetery for a place where bodies are kept.
mistakes.right: Kept is mortuary. Buried is cemetery.
Monks live in a monastery. Nuns live in a convent.

mistakes.wrong: Using the wrong group word (herd for lions).
mistakes.right: Name the animal first. Lions form a pride.
Learn each place with what it holds: coins mint, aircraft hangar.

subtopics.notes:
### Two simple shapes
1. **A place where ___ is kept or done.** The answer is a place word.
2. **A group of ___.** The answer is a collective noun.

Both are matching. The phrase names the thing, and you name its place or its group.

### Places
Match the place to what is kept or done there.
| Place | What happens there |
|---|---|
| apiary | bees are kept |
| aviary | birds are kept |
| aquarium | fish are kept |
| granary | grain is stored |
| stable | horses are kept |
| kennel | dogs are kept |
| armoury | weapons are stored |
| mint | coins are made |
| hangar | aircraft are kept and repaired |
| mortuary | dead bodies are kept |
| cemetery | the dead are buried |
| abattoir | animals are killed for meat |
| monastery | monks live |
| convent | nuns live |
| orphanage | orphans live |
| museum | historical objects are shown |
| observatory | stars are studied through telescopes |

> **Example:** A place where coins are made is a **mint**. A treasury keeps money but does not make coins.

### Look-alike places
- **apiary** (bees) and **aviary** (birds). Aviary goes with aviation and flying birds.
- **monastery** (monks, men) and **convent** (nuns, women).
- **mortuary** (bodies kept) and **cemetery** (bodies buried).
- **granary** (grain) and granite (a rock). Options often plant such neighbours.

> **Watch:** The hangar for aircraft is different from a hanger for clothes. Check the spelling.

### Groups
Collective nouns are memory work, but only a few come up.
| A group of | Word |
|---|---|
| lions | pride |
| wolves, dogs | pack |
| cattle | herd |
| sheep, birds | flock |
| bees | swarm |
| fish | school, shoal |
| ships | fleet |
| islands | archipelago |
| stars in a pattern | constellation |
| worshippers | congregation |
| musicians | orchestra, band |
| experts or judges | panel |
| soldiers | troop |

> **Rule:** Ask which animal or thing the phrase names before you look at the options. The animal decides the word.

### Worked examples
- *A place where grain is stored.* The object is grain, so the word is **granary**.
- *A group of sheep.* Sheep move in a **flock**. Cattle move in a herd.
- *A place where aircraft are kept and repaired.* The word is **hangar**.

Each one takes about ten seconds once the pairs are in memory.

### How to answer
1. Find the key noun: bees, coins, wolves, islands.
2. Recall its partner place or group word.
3. Check the look-alike before you mark.

Say the pairs aloud: bees and apiary, coins and mint, wolves and pack, islands and archipelago. The exam asks for the partner, never a definition.

patterns.name: Place where something is kept or made
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'a place where ___ are kept, stored or made'.
steps: Underline the object kept or made.
Recall the place word tied to it.
patterns.why: Each place word has a single stored object.

example.q: A place where bees are kept: (a) aviary (b) apiary (c) aquarium (d) granary
steps: Aviary is for birds and aquarium for fish.

patterns.name: Place named by the people in it
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'a place where monks live', 'where orphans live' or 'where animals are killed'.
steps: Underline who or what is there.
Match: monks monastery, nuns convent, orphans orphanage.
patterns.why: The people or the activity name the place.

example.q: A place where nuns live: (a) monastery (b) convent (c) orphanage (d) mortuary

patterns.name: Collective noun for animals
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'a group of lions, wolves, cattle, bees or sheep'.
steps: Reject words that belong to other animals.
patterns.why: The animal decides the word.

example.q: A group of lions: (a) pack (b) herd (c) pride (d) swarm
steps: Pack is for wolves, herd for cattle, swarm for bees.

patterns.name: Collective noun for things or people
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'a group of islands, stars, ships or worshippers'.
steps: Check the options for a near word.
patterns.why: Each non-animal group also has one fixed word.

example.q: A group of islands: (a) archipelago (b) constellation (c) fleet (d) panel
steps: Constellation is for stars and fleet for ships.

patterns.name: Look-alike place pairs
patterns.howToSpot: Two options are nearly the same place: mortuary and cemetery, monastery and convent, apiary and aviary.
steps: Find the pair in the options.
Read the detail word: kept or buried, men or women.
patterns.why: The look-alike is the planted wrong option.

example.q: A place where dead bodies are kept before burial: (a) cemetery (b) mortuary (c) abattoir (d) hangar
steps: A cemetery is where bodies are buried.
A mortuary is where they are kept.

revision: Places: apiary bees, aviary birds, granary grain, mint coins, hangar aircraft, mortuary bodies, abattoir slaughter.
Monastery is for monks. Convent is for nuns.
Groups: pride lions, pack wolves, herd cattle, flock sheep, swarm bees.
Fleet ships, archipelago islands, constellation stars.
Look-alikes: apiary/aviary, mortuary/cemetery, monastery/convent.

subtopics.title: Government systems, studies and word-craft
subtopics.concept: This group holds four word sets: forms of government, speech and writing, time and frequency, and 'that which cannot be ...' words. In each set the stem holds one key detail. Match the detail, then check the look-alike pair.

tricks.title: Ruler first
tricks.body: Circle the ruler in the stem before the options. It gives the word.

example.q: Government by officials: (a) bureaucracy (b) theocracy (c) anarchy (d) monarchy
steps: Theocracy is priests and monarchy is a king.

tricks.title: Three dead words
tricks.body: Learn elegy, eulogy and epitaph as one set. One question can ask any of them.

tricks.title: Link the verb
tricks.body: Pair each cannot-be word with its verb: read illegible, see invisible, hear inaudible.

mistakes.right: Mourning poem is elegy. Praise is eulogy. Tomb writing is epitaph.
Biannual is twice a year. Biennial is once in two years.
Cannot be read is illegible. Ineligible is not qualified.

mistakes.wrong: Using anarchy for a small ruling group.
mistakes.right: Anarchy is no government. A small group is oligarchy.

mistakes.wrong: Learning government words without the ruler.
mistakes.right: Learn each word with its ruler: rich, nobles, people, officials.

subtopics.notes:
### Government words: who rules?
Every government word answers one question: **who holds the power?** Find the ruler in the stem and match it.
| Ruled by | Word |
|---|---|
| the people | democracy |
| one person with total power | autocracy |
| a king or queen | monarchy |
| the rich | plutocracy |
| nobles, the upper class | aristocracy |
| a small group | oligarchy |
| paid officials | bureaucracy |
| religious leaders, in God's name | theocracy |
| the mob | mobocracy |
| ability and merit | meritocracy |
| nobody, no government | anarchy |

> **Example:** Government by the wealthy. Pluto means wealth. The word is **plutocracy**.

### Speech and writing words
These come in confusing pairs.
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| elegy | a poem of mourning for the dead |
| eulogy | words of praise, often after death |
| epitaph | words written on a tomb |
| soliloquy | speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone |
| extempore | spoken without preparation |
| prologue | the opening of a play or book |
| epilogue | the closing part |
| anthology | a collection of poems or stories |

> **Tip:** Learn the three dead words as a set. Mourning is elegy, praise is eulogy, tomb writing is epitaph.

### Time words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| annual | once a year |
| biannual | twice a year |
| biennial | once in two years |
| perennial | lasting through the years |
| decade, century, millennium | 10, 100, 1000 years |
| nocturnal | active at night |
| diurnal | active by day |

> **Rule:** -ennial counts years, so biennial is every two years. -annual counts times in a year, so biannual is twice a year.

### That which cannot be ...
These start with in-, il- or im-, which mean not. The verb in the stem decides.
| Cannot be | Word |
|---|---|
| read | illegible |
| seen | invisible |
| heard | inaudible |
| believed | incredible |
| avoided | inevitable |
| conquered | invincible |
| corrected | incorrigible |
| wiped out | indelible |

> **Watch:** Illegible means cannot be read. Ineligible means not qualified. They sound alike.

### Worked examples
- *Opening part of a play.* Pro- means before. The word is **prologue**.
- *Speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone.* The word is **soliloquy**.
- *Active at night.* The word is **nocturnal**. Active by day is diurnal.
- *That which cannot be avoided.* The word is **inevitable**.

Read the key word in each stem first. It gives the answer before you look at the options.

### How to answer
1. Decide the set: government, speech and writing, time, or cannot-be.
2. Find the key word: the ruler, the kind of writing, the number of years, or the verb.
3. Match it, then check the look-alike pair.

patterns.name: Government or rule by ...
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'government by', 'rule by', or 'a state with no government'.
steps: Match the ruler to the word in the table.
patterns.why: The ruler decides the word.

example.q: Government by the wealthy: (a) aristocracy (b) plutocracy (c) democracy (d) oligarchy
steps: Aristocracy is nobles and democracy is the people.

patterns.name: Speech and literary words
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase is about a poem, a speech, tomb writing, a life story or talking alone.
steps: Underline the kind of writing or speech.
Pick the word for that job.
patterns.why: Overlapping pairs make this set easy to mix up.

example.q: A speech or writing that praises someone: (a) elegy (b) eulogy (c) epitaph (d) epilogue
steps: Elegy is mourning. Epitaph is on a tomb.

patterns.name: Time and frequency words
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase gives how often (every two years, twice a year) or when (at night).
steps: Underline the count or the time.
Use -ennial for years and -annual for times a year.
patterns.why: The word part shows what is counted.

example.q: Once in two years: (a) annual (b) biannual (c) biennial (d) perennial
steps: Every two years is a count of years.
Biennial is once in two years.

patterns.name: That which cannot be ...
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase says 'that which cannot be read, seen, heard, conquered or corrected'.
steps: Recall the in- word for it.
patterns.why: The verb in the stem gives the word.

example.q: That which cannot be read: (a) illegible (b) ineligible (c) inaudible (d) invisible
steps: Inaudible is not heard and invisible is not seen.
Ineligible sounds alike but means not qualified.

patterns.name: Small-group and no-government rule
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase names a few rulers or no ruler at all.
steps: Underline how many rule: few or none.
Match: a small group is oligarchy, none is anarchy.
patterns.why: The number of rulers is the whole clue.

example.q: Rule by a small group of people: (a) anarchy (b) oligarchy (c) monarchy (d) theocracy
steps: The ruler is a small group.
Monarchy is one king or queen.

revision: Ruler decides: people democracy, rich plutocracy, officials bureaucracy, God theocracy, none anarchy.
Dead words: elegy mourning, eulogy praise, epitaph tomb.
Biannual is twice a year. Biennial is every two years.
Cannot-be: read illegible, conquer invincible, correct incorrigible, avoid inevitable.
Nocturnal is by night. Diurnal is by day.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy for one-word substitution
subtopics.concept: One-word substitution gives one or two quick marks in most papers. It is a memory topic, so the plan is to build a word bank by category and revise it every week. In the exam, classify the phrase, remove other families, and prefer the more specific word.

tricks.title: Specific beats general
tricks.body: If both a general and a specific word fit, choose the specific one. It matches the detail the examiner gave.

example.q: Killing of one's brother: (a) homicide (b) fratricide (c) patricide (d) suicide

tricks.title: Weekly weak list
tricks.body: Any word missed twice goes on a short list. Read only that list twice a week.

tricks.title: Syllable check for spelling
tricks.body: For spelling items say the word slowly in syllables and match each syllable to the option.

mistakes.wrong: Learning words in one long alphabet list.
mistakes.right: Learn by category and keep a personal sheet.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing the general word when a specific one is offered.
mistakes.right: Pick the word that matches the exact detail.
Epidemic is one area. Pandemic is many countries or the world.
Emigrant leaves. Immigrant comes in.
Say the word in syllables and match each part.

subtopics.notes:
### Where it fits
Most SSC, Railway and Banking papers have one or two of these items. Each takes about 15 seconds if you know the word. It is a **memory topic**, so plan a word bank.

### Build the bank by category
Do not learn a random alphabet list. Take one category at a time.
1. Killing (-cide) and fear (-phobia) words.
2. Study (-ology) words and people words.
3. Places and groups.
4. Government, speech, time and cannot-be words.
5. Medical words.
6. Direction and contrast pairs.

Words in one category support each other. Add every new word from mock tests to a **personal sheet** under its category.

### Daily 10-minute routine
- Read 10 new words and 20 old words aloud with their meanings.
- Every weekend, take a 30-word mixed self-test.
- Any word you miss twice goes on a **weak list**. Revise it weekly.

### Four steps in the exam
1. **Classify** the phrase: killing, fear, study, person, place, group, government or medical.
2. **Remove** options from other families. Two usually go here.
3. **Match** the exact detail: bees not birds, mother not father.
4. **Prefer the specific word.** For killing one's mother, matricide beats the general homicide.

> **Rule:** When two options fit, pick the one that matches the detail in the phrase.

### Medical words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| antidote | medicine against a poison |
| antiseptic | applied to wounds to stop infection |
| anaesthetic | removes the feeling of pain |
| antibiotic | medicine that kills bacteria |
| epidemic | disease spreading widely in one area |
| pandemic | disease spreading over many countries |
| endemic | disease always present in one area |
| convalescent | recovering after an illness |

### Direction and contrast pairs
| Pair | Difference |
|---|---|
| emigrant / immigrant | leaves a country / comes into a country |
| introvert / extrovert | turned inward / outgoing |
| amateur / professional | for pleasure / for pay |
| novice / veteran | beginner / very experienced |

### A worked check
Question: *the murder of one's mother.*
1. Classify: this is a killing word, so the suffix is -cide.
2. Remove options from other families, such as -phobia or -ology words.
3. Match the detail: mother is mater, so matricide.
4. Reject homicide. It is true but too general.

### Spelling-based items
Some questions say *select the correctly spelt word*. All four options are one word with different spellings. Know the word, then check the tricky letters. Say it in syllables: con-va-les-cent, a-the-ist, ob-so-lete.

> **Watch:** If two options remain and you are unsure, guess only if the paper has no negative marking. Otherwise use the specific-detail rule first.

patterns.name: Specific word beats the general word
patterns.howToSpot: Two options fit the family. One is general (homicide) and one matches the exact detail (matricide).
steps: Underline the detail in the phrase.
Find the option that names that detail.
patterns.why: The examiner rewards the word that fits the detail.

example.q: The murder of one's mother: (a) homicide (b) matricide (c) suicide (d) genocide

patterns.name: Medical and science words
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase is about a medicine, the spread of a disease, or recovery.
steps: Sort: area, world or always present for diseases.
patterns.why: Epidemic, endemic and pandemic differ only by spread.

example.q: A disease spreading over many countries: (a) epidemic (b) endemic (c) pandemic (d) antidote
steps: Many countries means a very wide spread.
Epidemic is one area and endemic is always present.

patterns.name: Correctly spelt substitute
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'select the correctly spelt word'. All options are one word spelt in four ways.
steps: Recall the word for the phrase.
Match each syllable against the options.
patterns.why: Syllables show which letters belong.

example.q: One who is recovering after illness: (a) convalscent (b) convalescent (c) convelescent (d) convalesent

patterns.name: Direction and contrast pairs
patterns.howToSpot: Options hold both members of a pair: emigrant and immigrant, introvert and extrovert.
steps: Read the direction or contrast in the phrase.
patterns.why: The partner is planted as a wrong option.

example.q: One who leaves his own country to settle in another: (a) immigrant (b) emigrant (c) extrovert (d) veteran
steps: The person is leaving his country.
An immigrant comes into a new country.

patterns.name: Classify, then remove families
patterns.howToSpot: The options come from four different families, and the phrase names only one of them.
steps: Name the family of the phrase.
patterns.why: Two options usually die at the classify step.

example.q: One who does a job for pleasure, not pay: (a) professional (b) amateur (c) novice (d) veteran
steps: Not for pay is the key detail.
Amateur is for pleasure. Professional is for pay.

revision: Bank by category, keep a personal sheet, revise a weekly weak list.
Four steps: classify, remove other families, match the detail, prefer the specific word.
Epidemic is one area. Pandemic is the world. Endemic is always present.
Emigrant leaves. Immigrant comes in.
Amateur is for pleasure. Professional is for pay.
Spelling items: break the word into syllables.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem begins 'One who...' or 'A person who...' and names a job, habit or nature; all four options are person words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Underline the exact detail in the stem — the object of the job (maps, children, dictionary) or the habit (drinks, wastes money, easily fooled). Then match the option that owns exactly that detail, and reject the partner word (widow/widower, miser/spendthrift) planted among the options.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *One who eats too much*
example.solution: **Glutton**. Gullible (easily cheated) and spendthrift (wastes money) are other person words that describe different habits.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'The killing of ...' and may or may not name a special victim (mother, brother, king, infant, race).
pyqPatterns.approach: Match the victim to its root: mater = mother, pater = father, frater = brother, geno = race. If no special victim is named, the general word homicide is right. All four options are usually -cide words, so the victim decides.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *The killing of an infant*
example.solution: **Infanticide**. Genocide would need a whole race as the victim; homicide names no victim at all.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'An abnormal fear of ...' points to a -phobia word; 'The study of ...' or 'The science of ...' points to a -logy word.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the family first (fear or study), then match the root to the thing feared or studied: hydro = water, acro = heights, ornitho = birds, entomo = insects, seismo = earthquakes. Watch the entomology/etymology twin.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *The study of birds*
example.solution: **Ornithology**. Entomology is insects — one letter group apart, which is exactly the confusion the examiner tests.

pyqPatterns.pattern: A place where ... / A group of ...
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem names a stored thing or resident ('A place where bees are kept') or a collection ('A group of wolves').
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the key noun and recall its fixed partner: bees → apiary, grain → granary, coins → mint, monks → monastery, wolves → pack, lions → pride, islands → archipelago. Check the one-letter traps (apiary/aviary) and the partner-place traps (monastery/convent) before marking.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A place where birds are kept*
example.solution: **Aviary**. Apiary (bees) differs by one letter and is always planted beside it.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Government by ...' or 'Rule by ...' followed by the ruler — the people, the rich, officials, God, a king, nobody.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the ruler in the stem and match it: people → democracy, rich → plutocracy, officials → bureaucracy, God → theocracy, one person → autocracy, a few → oligarchy, none → anarchy. The first part of each word names the ruler.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *Government by officials*
example.solution: **Bureaucracy**. The ruler here is the office machinery, not the people (democracy) or the rich (plutocracy).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is about a poem, speech, tomb writing, life story, or about how often something happens.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide what the writing does (mourns → elegy, praises → eulogy, marks a tomb → epitaph, own life → autobiography). For frequency apply the counting rule: -ennial counts years (biennial = every two years), -annual counts times per year (biannual = twice a year).

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A speech praising a person who has died*
example.solution: **Eulogy**. It praises; an elegy mourns. The two are always planted together.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is about a medicine (against poison, germs, pain) or about a disease's spread (one area, the whole world, always present).
pyqPatterns.approach: For medicines, fix the job: against poison → antidote, kills bacteria inside → antibiotic, cleans wounds outside → antiseptic, removes feeling → anaesthetic. For diseases fix the spread: one area now → epidemic, the world → pandemic, always in one area → endemic.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A disease spreading rapidly in one area*
example.solution: **Epidemic**. Pandemic would need many countries; endemic is the constant-presence word, not rapid spread.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'Select the correctly spelt word ...' and all four options are the same word in different spellings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the word from the meaning, then break it into syllables and check each part against the options. Watch the classic slips: ie/ei order, -ent/-ant endings, single or double letters (convalescent, atheist, obsolete).

example.q: Correctly spelt word for *one who walks in his sleep*: somnambulist / somnambulyst / somnabulist / somnambulast
example.solution: **Somnambulist** — somn (sleep) + ambul (walk) + ist. Only the -ist ending and the u after ambul are correct.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Murder of a king
solvedExamples.solution: The stem is a killing word (-cide family). Within the family, the object decides: rex/reg = king → **regicide**. *Homicide* is killing of a human in general, *genocide* of a race, *infanticide* of an infant — all real words planted as family-mates.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Family first (-cide), then the root object (rex = king).

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
solvedExamples.solution: Place stems are anchored by the stored object: bees → **apiary**. *Aviary* is the one-letter neighbour (birds), *aquarium* holds fish, *granary* grain.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Stored-object anchor: bees → apiary. Watch the aviary trap.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts poison
solvedExamples.solution: The anti- options form the family; the function decides: counteracts poison → **antidote**. *Antibiotic* kills bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents infection on wounds, *anaesthetic* removes sensation.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Function matching within the anti- family.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who loves books
practice.solution: Biblio = book + phile = lover → **bibliophile**. *Philatelist* collects stamps, *lexicographer* compiles dictionaries, *philanthropist* loves humankind through charity.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who talks in his sleep
practice.solution: Somni = sleep + loqui = speak → **somniloquist**. *Somnambulist* walks in sleep (ambul = walk) — the classic sibling trap; *insomniac* cannot sleep at all.
practice.shortcut: somni- (sleep) + verb root decides: walk vs speak.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by the people through their elected representatives
practice.solution: Demos = people + cracy = rule → **democracy**. The stem names the ruler ('the people'); the other options name one ruler, officials, and nobles respectively.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can use both hands with equal ease
practice.solution: Ambi = both + dextr = right hand/skill → **ambidextrous**. *Ambivalent* means having mixed feelings, *amphibious* means living on land and water — the ambi-/amphi- family tempts, the dextr root decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
practice.solution: Bees are kept in an **apiary**; *aviary* (one letter away) keeps birds, *aquarium* fish, *granary* grain.
practice.shortcut: Stored-object anchor; the aviary trap is deliberate.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The act of killing one's own brother
practice.solution: Frater = brother → **fratricide**. *Patricide* kills the father, *regicide* the king, *genocide* a whole community — all -cide family-mates separated by the relation root.
practice.shortcut: Family root decides the relation: frater = brother.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A speech delivered without any preparation
practice.solution: Unprepared speech = **extempore**. *Epilogue* closes a play, *monologue* is a long one-person speech (prepared or not), *elocution* is the art of clear speaking.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who studies the stars and other heavenly bodies scientifically
practice.solution: The word 'scientifically' fixes **astronomer** — the scientist of the sky. *Astrologer* predicts fates from star positions; *cosmonaut* travels; *geologist* studies the earth.
practice.shortcut: Science vs prediction: astronomer vs astrologer — the stem's adjective decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of enclosed spaces
practice.solution: Claustro = enclosed → **claustrophobia**. The family: hydro- water, acro- heights, xeno- foreigners — the stem names the feared object and the suffix names the family.
practice.shortcut: phobia family; match the feared object.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Words inscribed on a tomb
practice.solution: Tomb inscription = **epitaph**. *Epilogue* ends a play, *elegy* mourns in verse, *epigram* is a witty short saying — the epi- family is planted wholesale.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person appointed to hear both sides and settle a dispute
practice.solution: An **arbitrator** is the authorised settler of disputes. *Agitator* stirs trouble, *dictator* rules absolutely, *philanthropist* gives to charity — different families entirely.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of lions
practice.solution: Lions live in a **pride**. *Herd* suits cattle, *swarm* bees, *flock* sheep or birds — the four collective options are swapped around in every paper.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is present everywhere at the same time
practice.solution: Omni = all + present → **omnipresent**. The omni-triplet: -potent (power), -scient (knowledge), -present (place) — the stem names the dimension.
practice.shortcut: Omni- family: match the ending to the stem's dimension (place → present).

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts the effects of poison
practice.solution: Counteracts poison = **antidote**. *Antibiotic* attacks bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents wound infection, *anaesthetic* kills sensation during surgery.
practice.shortcut: anti- family; function match: poison → antidote.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

That which cannot be avoided
practice.solution: Cannot be avoided = **inevitable**. Link each option to its verb: conquer→invincible, see→invisible, believe→incredible. The stem's verb ('avoided') picks its partner.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of one's own mother
practice.solution: mater = mother, so killing of the mother = **matricide**. Patricide is the father, fratricide the brother; no special victim is named in genocide.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of a whole race or community
practice.solution: geno = race, so killing of a whole race = **genocide**. Homicide is a general killing of a human being; the stem names a race.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of heights
practice.solution: acro = height, so fear of heights = **acrophobia**. Hydrophobia is fear of water, xenophobia of foreigners, agoraphobia of open or crowded places.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of water
practice.solution: hydro = water, so fear of water = **hydrophobia**. Nyctophobia is fear of darkness, photophobia fear of light.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The scientific study of insects
practice.solution: entomo = insect, so the study of insects = **entomology**. Etymology (word origins) is the classic one-letter-group trap; ornithology is birds.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The scientific study of earthquakes
practice.solution: seismo = earthquake, so **seismology**. Archaeology studies the past by digging; anthropology studies humankind.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The practice of having more than one spouse at the same time
practice.solution: poly = many + gamy = marriage → **polygamy**. Monogamy is one spouse; misogamy is hatred of marriage, misogyny hatred of women.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who collects stamps as a hobby
practice.solution: A stamp collector = **philatelist**. A numismatist collects coins; a bibliophile loves books; a philanderer is a man who flirts.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who draws maps
practice.solution: Maps → **cartographer**. The -grapher options are job words for other objects: beautiful writing, dance movements and films.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A doctor who treats diseases of children
practice.solution: Children → **paediatrician**. The others treat skin, heart and the mind.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who compiles a dictionary
practice.solution: lexicon = dictionary, so its maker is a **lexicographer**. A demographer studies population statistics.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who never drinks alcohol
practice.solution: Total abstainer from alcohol = **teetotaller**. A glutton overeats; a spendthrift wastes money; an ascetic lives a strict simple life, which is broader than abstaining from drink.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is easily cheated or deceived
practice.solution: One who believes too readily and is easily fooled = **gullible**. A sceptic doubts everything — almost the opposite; a cynic expects selfish motives; a pessimist expects the worst.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A woman whose husband has died
practice.solution: The man who has lost his wife is a widower; the woman is a **widow**. The pair word is the planted trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who spends money wastefully
practice.solution: Wasteful spender = **spendthrift**. A miser saves excessively and hates spending — the opposite partner; a hoarder piles things up; a steward manages another's household.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can speak many languages
practice.solution: poly = many + glot = tongue → **polyglot**. A polymath knows many subjects, not languages; a monoglot speaks only one — the planted opposite.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who hates women
practice.solution: mis = hate + gyn = woman → **misogynist**. A misanthrope hates mankind in general; a misogamist hates marriage.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where grain is stored
practice.solution: Grain → **granary**. Aviary is for birds, apiary for bees, arsenal for weapons — all stored-thing places for other things.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where aircraft are kept and repaired
practice.solution: Aircraft → **hangar**. 'Hanger' (one who/that which hangs clothes) is the spelling trap; a dockyard serves ships.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where weapons and ammunition are stored
practice.solution: Weapons → **arsenal**. A mortuary keeps dead bodies; a mint makes coins.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where monks live as a community
practice.solution: Monks (men) → **monastery**; nuns (women) → convent. A seminary trains priests; an orphanage houses orphans.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where coins are manufactured
practice.solution: Coins are made at a **mint**. A treasury keeps public money but does not make coins; a refinery processes oil or ore.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where stars and planets are studied with telescopes
practice.solution: Stars studied through telescopes → **observatory**. A planetarium is a domed hall that shows an artificial sky; it is not a study place.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A large group of bees flying together
practice.solution: Bees → **swarm**. Flock is for sheep or birds, herd for cattle, pack for wolves or dogs.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of wolves
practice.solution: Wolves hunt in a **pack**. Lions take pride, cattle take herd, bees swarm.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of stars forming a fixed pattern
practice.solution: A fixed pattern of stars = a **constellation** (like the Great Bear). A galaxy is a vast system of millions of stars, not a named pattern.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of ships sailing together
practice.solution: Ships → **fleet**. Flock is for birds or sheep; a bouquet is a bunch of flowers.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of islands lying close together
practice.solution: A cluster of islands = **archipelago**. A peninsula is land almost surrounded by water — the planted geography look-alike.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by the rich
practice.solution: pluto = wealth → rule by the rich = **plutocracy**. Democracy is rule by the people, autocracy by one person, bureaucracy by officials.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by religious leaders who claim to rule in the name of God
practice.solution: theo = God → **theocracy**. Monarchy is rule by a king; anarchy is the absence of any rule.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A state of society with no government and no law
practice.solution: an = without + archy = rule → **anarchy**, lawlessness. Oligarchy is rule by a few; autonomy is self-rule of a region within a state.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A poem of mourning for the dead
practice.solution: A sad poem mourning the dead = **elegy**. A eulogy is a speech or writing that praises the dead — mourns vs praises is the trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The story of a person's life written by the person himself
practice.solution: auto = self → written by oneself = **autobiography**. A biography is written by another person; an anthology is a collection of poems or stories; an almanac is a yearly book of dates and facts.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Happening once in two years
practice.solution: The -ennial family counts years: once in two years = **biennial**. Biannual means twice in one year — the classic trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Animals that remain active at night
practice.solution: Active at night = **nocturnal** (owl, bat). Diurnal animals are active by day; aquatic live in water; arboreal live in trees.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Handwriting that cannot be read
practice.solution: Cannot be read = **illegible**. Ineligible means not qualified — the sound-alike trap; illiterate means unable to read or write; inaudible cannot be heard.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

That which cannot be conquered or defeated
practice.solution: vinc = conquer (as in victory) → cannot be conquered = **invincible**. Invisible cannot be seen; inevitable cannot be avoided; incorrigible cannot be corrected.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of one human being by another
practice.solution: No special victim is named, only 'a human being' (homi = man), so the general word **homicide** is right. The stem is not about a race, king or oneself.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A disease that spreads over many countries and the whole world
practice.solution: pan = all → world-wide spread = **pandemic**. An epidemic spreads fast but stays within one area; endemic is always present in one area; quarantine is a period of isolation, not a disease word.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A child whose parents are dead
practice.solution: The exact single word is **orphan**. 'Bereaved' only means having lost someone — the general word the specific-word rule beats; a widow lost a husband; a hermit lives alone by choice.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that destroys bacteria inside the body
practice.solution: **Antibiotics** are taken to kill bacteria within. An antidote works against a poison, an antiseptic cleans wounds from outside, an anaesthetic removes the feeling of pain.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A disease that is always present in a particular area or among a particular people
practice.solution: en = in → always present within one area = **endemic**. Epidemic and pandemic describe sudden spread, not constant presence; contagious means spreading by contact.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A drug that takes away the feeling of pain during an operation
practice.solution: an = without + aisthesis = feeling → **anaesthetic** removes sensation. The other anti- words fight germs or poison, not pain.

practice.q:
Select the correctly spelt word that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who does not believe in the existence of God
practice.solution: The correct spelling is **atheist**: athe + ist. The other options swap the ie/ei letters or distort the syllables.

practice.q:
Select the correctly spelt word that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is recovering health after an illness
practice.solution: **Convalescent** — say it in syllables: con-va-les-cent. The ending is -escent, and the third syllable keeps the s before c.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who is outgoing and mixes freely with others
practice.solution: extro = outward → interested in what is outside = **extrovert**. An introvert is turned inward; a recluse and a misanthrope avoid people altogether.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who comes into a foreign country to live there permanently
practice.solution: im/in = in → one who comes IN = **immigrant**. An emigrant leaves his own country (e-/ex- = out); the same person is an emigrant there and an immigrant here.
